hook: Does a short night make you slower the next morning? A sports science class measured 14 students: hours of sleep and reaction time on a screen test. A list of 28 numbers says little. Plot each student as one point, sleep across and reaction time up, and a clear pattern appears at once.

prereq.q: In a study of whether study time affects test scores, which is the response variable?
prereq.why: The response is the outcome the study measures; study time is the explanatory variable.
A quantitative variable takes numerical values that can be averaged.

figure.caption: Each point is one student. Sleep goes across (explanatory), reaction time up (response). Pattern: strong, negative, linear.

chain.cause: Two quantitative variables are measured on the same individuals
chain.effect: plot one point per individual: explanatory variable on the horizontal axis, response on the vertical axis

chain.cause: Look at how $y$ changes as $x$ increases
chain.effect: direction: positive (up together), negative (one up, one down) or none

chain.cause: Look at the shape and the scatter around it
chain.effect: form (linear or curved) and strength (how closely points follow the form)

chain.cause: Look for points away from the pattern
chain.effect: unusual features: outliers and clusters, which deserve a reason, and then describe it all in context

ideas: A scatterplot shows the relationship between two quantitative variables measured on the same individuals.
Describe direction, form, strength and unusual features, in context: "a strong, negative, linear association between hours of sleep and reaction time, with no outliers".
Strength is how closely points follow the pattern, not how steep it is; a curved pattern can be strong.
Association is not causation: observational data show a pattern, not its cause.

misconception.wrong: A steep trend in a scatterplot means a strong association.
misconception.right: Steepness and strength are different. Strength is how tightly the points cluster around the pattern; a gentle trend with little scatter is stronger than a steep trend with lots of scatter.

summary: A scatterplot plots two quantitative variables, explanatory on the horizontal axis and response on the vertical. Describe what you see with four features in context: direction, form, strength and unusual features such as outliers. A pattern in observational data shows association, not cause.
